Split the requirements of stage S11 (Self-managing swarm (lane health, self-healing, machine watchdog, shared queue, smart routing, quota forecasting, daily phone summary)) of "Project Swarm roadmap (audit 2026-10-20)" into small build tickets.
Return ONE JSON file named by the job output: a JSON array of ticket objects, nothing else.
Each ticket object has these fields:
key (short unique name in this file), title (under 140 characters), type (build, test, docs, migration, design, contract or human),
epic (a feature group name), scopeRefs (requirement ids, at least one for build, test, docs, migration), acceptance (1 to 5 observable checks; required for build, test, migration),
files (the files this ticket writes: repo-relative paths WITH their folders, for example src/app/page.tsx or supabase/migrations/0001_init.sql, never a bare file name unless the file really lives at the repo root; the scope header may allow additional exact root names with `Root files: a.json, b.txt`; never a folder, never an absolute path, never a dot-env file: use env.example.txt for an env template), deletes (existing files this ticket must delete, each named exactly; omit when none), dependencies (new npm packages the ticket needs, like zod or zod@^3.23.0; the runner installs them and the change goes through the security gate; omit when none), context (files it reads), contracts (contract files it uses), tests (the test files that prove this ticket: a build ticket lists the test files owned by its test ticket and depends on that test ticket; a test ticket lists its own), screens (only on UI tickets: the ids of the design screens the ticket renders, from the profile ui screens), dependsOn (keys of other tickets in this file, or ids of existing open tickets when listed below),
size (S or M; never larger: split instead), risk (low, medium or high), sensitive (true for payments, auth or customer data), steps (only for human tickets: 1 to 30 short imperative steps), skeleton (true only on the tickets of the thinnest vertical slice of the first stage: database, API, screen and test, the smallest path through the product; omit it elsewhere).
Rules: no ticket may gate more than 8 others: shared work (shared CSS, layout, i18n keys, types) is split early into one small ticket per component or file group, so one blocked ticket cannot hold half a stage; every requirement is covered by at least one ticket; every ticket traces to a requirement; two open tickets that can run at the same time never write the same file unless one depends on the other (dependsOn);
put shared types or contracts first and make the tickets that use them depend on them; add a test ticket for each requirement group.
Every build, test and migration ticket has at least one acceptance line (copy the requirement's own acceptance line when you have nothing more exact). A test never runs before the module it imports exists: prefer listing a module's test files in that build ticket's "tests" field over a separate test ticket, and when a separate test ticket is needed it is written to run after the build tickets it tests (the runner orders it after them).
A ticket of type contract writes exactly one OpenAPI 3 JSON file under contracts/ (for example contracts/api.json) using only paths (get, post, put, patch, delete, each with an operationId), components.schemas and local $ref; TypeScript, SQL and YAML types belong in build tickets that depend on the contract ticket.
Migration tickets write DDL only; their tests are separate tickets in a tests folder.
Keep every ticket small enough for one worker answer: at most 4 files, each file under about 12 KB when written; split a bigger feature into several tickets (the output of one worker is capped at about 15 KB per file).
Tools: when an acceptance check or test runs a tool command (supabase, cypress, prisma, drizzle-kit), a ticket must write that tool's config file (for example supabase/config.toml, cypress.config.ts) unless the project already has it.
Wiring rule: for every requirement that has build tickets, add ONE integration ticket (type build, "integration": true) that mounts those modules in the real routes, pages or entry points (for example src/app/.../page.tsx, a router file, an API route file) so a user can reach the feature.
Its "tests" lists a route-level or end-to-end test that requests the real route or page and checks the result (not a unit test of one module); its acceptance names the route or page; its scopeRefs are the requirement ids; its files are the route and page files only.
You do not need to list its dependsOn on the module tickets of the same requirement: the runner adds them. Two integration tickets that edit the same shared file (router, navigation, layout) are chained by the runner, the later one after the earlier.
A requirement is done only when its integration ticket is done and its route-level test passed.
Root rules (follow exactly in addition to the rules above):
1. Never put a file in a ticket's context or reads unless it exists in the repo now or is produced by a ticket in its dependsOn chain (the producer must be an ancestor).
2. Two tickets in the same wave never write the same file: chain them with dependsOn or merge them.
3. A test ticket is never in a later stage or wave than the code it tests: put tests in the build ticket's own outputs, or a test ticket that dependsOn it in the same stage.
4. Protected files (coordination/checks.json, .project-swarm.json, .swarm/, .git/ and the project's protected paths) are never assigned to worker tickets: route them to an owner-window human ticket.
5. Every requirement with build tickets gets exactly one integration ticket that mounts the modules in the real entry point (route, CLI command or page) with a route-level or end-to-end test.

Work only from the requirements below.

R-081: Every lane is health-monitored automatically from the config and the adapter registry, with no hardcoded lane list.
  - A monitor inside autopilot probes every lane found in the config (every lanes key and every local endpoint) and in the adapter registry on a timer of about 2 minutes, and records healthy, degraded, down or paused with a reason and a last-checked time.
  - A test config that adds a fake new lane shows it monitored, on probation, then routed, with zero manual setup; removing a lane from the config removes it from monitoring and routing and leaves nothing pointing at it.
  - Probes are free checks only (tunnel or port reachable, a models-list GET, a CLI version or status call, rate-limit records, spend-cap records); a test asserts no model call and no POST is made by any probe.
R-082: Every lane adapter ships a health check, and new lanes start on probation.
  - The adapter interface includes a health function; a contract test fails for any adapter without one, so it cannot ship.
  - A lane with no specific check uses the default: endpoint or CLI reachable plus the last job result.
  - A new lane takes small jobs only until it passes 3 checks and 2 real jobs, then joins full routing automatically.
R-083: Routing uses lane health and reroutes without stuck jobs.
  - A down lane gets no new jobs; its share goes to the next cheapest healthy lane in the existing cost order; a degraded lane stays routable with lower weight.
  - A job already running on a lane that goes down is retried on another lane; a test with a fake lane going down proves no job stays running.
  - A lane returns after 2 healthy checks in a row; flapping lanes back off for longer before they are re-added.
R-084: Lane status is visible and only truly stuck cases alert the owner.
  - Swarm Watch and Command Center show each lane with a colour dot and the reason; lane up and down events are written to the swarm event log and to the swarm message bus when it exists so every orchestrator sees the same status.
  - Needs-you is raised only when every lane in a tier has been down for 30 minutes, or a lane needs the owner (login expired, billing).
R-085: Lanes try safe self-healing before they are marked down.
  - Before marking a lane down the swarm tries only safe fixes: restart that lane's own tunnel or service, kill only that lane's own leaked processes (checked by command line and port), and wait out a rate-limit reset.
  - Only an expired login or a billing problem goes to Needs-you; every fix attempt is logged with the lane, the action and the result.
  - Tests with a fake tunnel that comes back after a restart, a fake leaked process, and a fake rate limit prove the fixes and prove that no unrelated process is touched.
R-086: A machine watchdog keeps every machine healthy and widens waves again when pressure drops.
  - The watchdog watches memory, swap, disk and orphaned swarm processes on each machine and cleans up automatically (only processes it can prove are leaked swarm test or lane processes; never other programs).
  - Waves shrink under memory pressure and widen again within 2 checks after pressure drops; a fake-machine test proves both directions and the orphan cleanup.
  - Disk use of the scratch and run folders stays under a configured cap through safe garbage collection that never touches a checkout holding swarm state.
R-087: The MacBook and the Mac mini pull from one shared queue.
  - Machines share one ledger and queue over the swarm message bus; any machine with free capacity takes the next ready ticket, with no hand-written wave manifests.
  - A claim is a lease with an expiry; two machines never run the same ticket; a crashed machine's lease expires and the ticket is retried. A two-fake-machine test proves no double run, including under a simulated crash and a network split.
  - Stage ownership by hand is no longer needed after this ships; held tickets return to the shared queue.
R-088: Smart routing picks the best-value healthy lane and keeps the safety rules.
  - The swarm tracks each lane's success rate, speed and cost per ticket type and routes each ticket to the best-value healthy lane, with the cost order as the tie-break.
  - No secrets go to any worker and no sensitive or production code goes to OpenRouter; tests with fake lanes prove these rules still hold under every routing score.
  - Routing decisions are logged with the scores that decided them.
R-089: Quota forecasting shifts work early and never raises a cap.
  - The swarm predicts when Claude subscription quotas, the Anthropic API daily cap and the OpenRouter daily cap will run out and shifts work to other lanes before they do.
  - A forecast never raises a cap and never spends more than the configured caps; a test proves a cap is never changed by forecasting or routing.
  - The forecast appears in the daily summary and on the board with its inputs labelled.
R-090: One short daily summary reaches the owner's phone.
  - Each morning one short message lists what shipped, lane health, spend per tier, and anything that truly needs the owner, and is sent to the phone through swarm phone or the inbox, not only the board.
  - A test with fake data proves the message content, its length limit and that it is sent once per day.
R-091: Self-management changes are reviewed and released safely.
  - Every change that kills processes, changes routing, or touches money or quotas gets an Opus static review before merge.
  - Each feature ships in a numbered release with tests that use fake lanes and fake machines, and the release is installed on both Macs and confirmed.
